title: What Made You Great Is Keeping You Stuck Leadership By Title Only
author: By Title Only
summary: The author introduces the Pattern-Environment Loop: the mechanism by which a leader's behavior creates an environment that then reinforces that exact behavior, turning former strengths into structural traps. Using a personal story about division of household labor and three client examples (micromanaging VP, approval-bottleneck founder, indispensable COO), he shows how the pattern always started as a genuine strength that earned rewards -- thoroughness, decisiveness, reliability -- and then calcified into an environment that made the original pattern necessary. A Harvard Business School paper on training failure ('The Great Training Robbery') establishes why awareness alone cannot break the loop: if the environment doesn't change, any behavioral change will revert. The fix is not to change behavior directly but to change the environment so the pattern is no longer required.
points: The Pattern-Environment Loop means you are not stuck in a pattern because you are weak -- you are stuck because the pattern used to be your strength and your environment won't let you stop, since it was built on the assumption you would never stop.

Corporate training fails at a rate that justifies a Harvard paper calling it 'The Great Training Robbery' because training changes behavior without changing the environment -- and the gravitational pull of the existing environment reverts behavior every time.

Micromanagement is not a personality flaw but an architectural outcome: the team stopped checking their own errors because the leader always caught them, making the leader's review the actual quality control system -- and removing the leader collapses the system, not because the leader was needed but because the environment requires it.

Fixing the behavior without fixing the environment produces the thing leaders dread most: they try to delegate, quality drops immediately, and this is taken as proof they were right to micromanage -- when it is actually proof that the environment was built to require them.
The diagnostic question is not 'what behavior should I change' but 'what would have to change in the environment -- not my behavior, the environment -- for this pattern to stop being required?'
quotes: Your behavior creates an environment, which supports the behavior, which strengthens the environment, and on and on it goes.

A Harvard Business School paper called 'The Great Training Robbery' found that most corporate training fails to produce lasting change, because the gravitational pull of the existing environment reverts people back to their previous behaviors. In other words, if the environment doesn't change, any behavioral change won't last.

Every single action feels like the right response to the situation. But every single action is also creating the environment that perpetuates the behavior. You're not stuck in a pattern because you're weak. You're stuck because the pattern used to be your strength and your environment won't let you stop.

Why should they spend an hour polishing the particulars of a deck when they know you will rewrite the darn thing anyway? Your behavior created a new environment. One where your review was the actual quality control, and everyone else's work just became the initial draft.

You don't break a Pattern-Environment Loop by changing your behavior. You break it by changing the environment. The micromanager doesn't need to trust the team more. They need an environment where the team's work matters before it reaches their desk.
The thing you think makes you indispensable is actually the thing that's keeping you stuck. Your strengths built the ball and chain, but your environment locked it around your ankle.
